speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: REFERENCE TO DECISION OF MR. SPEAKER, OCTOBER 29, ON MOTION FOR LEAVE TO INTRODUCE BILL
speechtext:
With reference to the remarks made yesterday by the hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) regarding the report in the debates and in Votes and Proceedings of my decision on the introduction of the bill to amend the Judges Act, sponsored by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), there is nothing unusual in the decision not being recorded in exactly the same words in these two reports.
It sometimes happens that the authorities are not at hand when a ruling has to be given from the chair, and it is necessarily given in a summary manner. It is afterwards reported in a less condensed form in Votes and Proceedings, which is the only official report of the things done and passed in the House of Commons, while Hansard is the official report of speeches.
The same practice obtains in courts of justice when a judge renders a judgment from the bench and then writes it up for the record. The main point is that the decision must not be altered. In this instance both Votes and Proceedings and debates report that the introduction of the bill was not permitted because it involved the expenditure of money. It cannot be said that my decision debars members from moving reductions in committee of supply, for that committee considers estimates brought down by the government and recommended by the crown. The government in that case takes the initiative.
Under section 54 of the British North America Act, no part of the public revenue can be appropriated to any purpose that has not been recommended by his excellency, and under standing order 60 no resolution for any public aid or charge upon the people can be presented on the day entered upon, but it must be adjourned and then referred to the committee of the whole. It does not matter whether the charge is an original amount, an increase or a reduction, no private member can introduce a money bill and skip the submission of a resolution to the committee of the whole.
Even if the bill were sponsored by the government it could not be introduced without a previous resolution. Mr. Speaker White decided in 1892, and his decision has held good ever since, that an amendment cannot be put when it disposes of the public revenue without the recommendation of the crown as required by the British North America Act of 1867.
The effect of the passage of the bill as presented by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would be immediate obligation to pay; no future legislation would be necessary, and therefore the authority cited last night by the hon. member does not apply. It is needless to add that any comparison with this bill and the committee of supply is irrelevant, and private members will be free in the future as they always have been to move any reduction in, and even to reject, any of the estimates brought down by the government.
I hope it will be understood that I am not now giving a decision on the introduction of the bill. This I did yesterday. I am now only making a statement in pursuance of the remarks made yesterday by the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. The house I am sure will readily understand that there being no motion before the Chair, the incident is closed and the house shall now proceed with its business.

Opposition):	Mr. Speaker, may I take this
opportunity to thank Your Honour for your usual courteous consideration of the point I raised yesterday. As for myself I accept your ruling. If I interpret what you had to say correctly, I think the house will be pleased to note that your ruling will not interfere with any private member moving in committee of supply for the reduction of items of expenditures.

speakeroldname: Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: TRIAL OF MAJOR-GENERAL KURT MEYER BY CANADIAN MILITARY COURT
speechtext:
I should like to inform the house that preliminary proceedings have now been taken for the trial of Brigade-fuhrer

(Major-General) Kurt Meyer, Commander of the 12th SS Panzer division (Hitler Jngend) during the fighting in Normandy in June, July and August of 1944. Major General Meyer will be tried by a Canadian military court convened pursuant to the war crimes regulations (Canada) of which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) informed the house on September 13, 1945.
Meyer will stand trial on seven charges having to do with the murder of forty-eight Canadian prisoners of war during the fighting in which the 3rd Canadian infantry division was engaged in the vicinity of Caen in June, 1944. He is charged specifically with having directed his troops to deny quarter in contravention of the laws and usages of war; to have been directly responsible, while a regimental or brigade commander, for the killing of seven prisoners at his headquarters; and to have been indirectly responsible for the deaths of eleven other prisoners at his headquarters, for twenty-three shot at the village of Authie, and also for seven later executed at Mouen after he had become divisional commander.
Meyer has been taken into custody of the Canadian military authorities and placed, pending trial, in the charge of Lieutenant Colonel R. P. Clark, D.S.O., commanding officer of the Royal Winnipeg rifles, Canadian army occupation force in Germany. Lieutenant Colonel B. J. S. Macdonald, O.B.E., E.D., head of the war crimes unit at Canadian military headquarters London, will be the chief prosecutor at the trial which is expected to begin on November 28, 1945, thus allowing Meyer four weeks in which to prepare his defence. Colonel Peter Wright, O.B.E., has been detailed by the Canadian army to act as defence counsel.
The members of the military court will be: Major General H. W. Foster, C.B.E., D.S.O., president, and members Major General R. H. Keefler, C.B.E., D.S.O., E.D., and Brigadiers
I.	S. Johnston, D.S.O., E.D., H. A. Sparling, D.S.O., H. P. Bell-Irving, D.S.O., O.B.E., with Brigadiers T. G. Gibson, D.S.O., and M. P. Bogert, D.S.O., O.B.E. as waiting members. The judge advocate will be Lieutenant Colonel W. B. Bredin, D.J.A.G., Canadian occupation force. The trial will be held at the marine barracks in Aurich, in the north western portion of the Canadian area of occupation in Germany.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
1 and 2. The sterling area countries which received- Mutual Aid from Canada included the United Kingdom, Australi-a, New Zealand, India and the crown colonies in the West Indies. All of these areas are no-w buying supplies from Canad-a, either paying directly in cash or through undertaking to reimburse the government of Canada for expenditures made on their -behalf.
The government of Canada is purchasing supplies in Canad-a as the agent of the governments of the United- Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand and India in response to requests from those governments. These are the countries in the sterling area receiving such assistance, and the question appears to relate only to the sterling area. Similar action is being taken, however, it may -be added, on -behalf of France, the Netherlands and the U.S.S.R. The government of Canada is assuming temporarily the costs of paying for these supplies it buys as agent and the governments of the other countries concerned have undertaken to reimburse the government for the expenditures so incurred. This was the principal method of postponing payment to which reference was made in the statement of the Minister of Finance on which this question was based. The government takes such action under the authority of section 3 of the War Appropriation Act, 1945.
The other "purely temporary expedients" contemplated in that statement and put into effect have consisted only in purchasing some time in advance the sterling exchange required to meet disbursements of the Canadian government in the sterling area, such as the pay of Canadian servicemen. The effect of such action is to increase temporarily the Canadian dollars being received by the United Kingdom exchange control and-, of course, there will be a corresponding reduction later when these balances are disbursed. This expedient provides dollars directly to the United Kingdom, but other countries of the sterling area benefit through being able to purchase these dollars from the United Kingdom for sterling.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: ORDERS IN COUNCIL AND TREASURY BOARD MINUTES
speechtext: For a copy of all orders in. council and treasury board minutes approved by His Excellency the Governor General since the 6th day of September, 1945.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Acting Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ORDERS IN COUNCIL AND TREASURY BOARD MINUTES
speechtext:
This motion raises an important question of principle, and I should like to say a few words on it. A motion of this kind has never been passed in this house, though similar motions have been made on at least two previous occasions. Nor can I find that a motion of this kind has ever been passed in any other parliamentary assembly in the British empire, though there may have been exceptions in local assemblies. The motion is for copies of all orders in council passed since the 6th day of September, 1945. That is to say, it is a request for authority to obtain copies of all orders in council passed within the last two months and, in addition, all treasury board decisions and minutes approved by the governor in council. It does not specify the particular subject or subjects in relation to which my hon. friend desires information. It does not refer to any particular class of orders. It is simply an unlimited request for all orders in council that have been passed.
In the first place I may state that to comply with an order of this kind would involve a great deal of expense and a great deal of labour on the part of the public service. It might establish a precedent which might be very serious if it were followed on subsequent occasions. With regard to the authorities on the subject, it will be found that there is no mention of anything of the kind by writers on matters of parliamentary practice and procedure. Hon. members will find the following reference in Todd's Parliamentary Government in England, volume 1, page 440:
Considerations of public policy, and a due regard to the interests of the state, occasionally demand, however, that information sought for by members of the legislature should be withheld, at the discretion and upon the general
Orders in Council Minutes

responsibility of ministers. This principle is systematically recognized in all parliamentary transactions: were it otherwise, it would be impossible to carry on the government with safety and honour. Whenever it is declared, by the responsible servant of the crown, that any information sought for in parliament could not be supplied without inconvenience to the public service, or for other sufficient reasons, the house refrains from insisting upon its production.
The two previous occasions in this house when similar motions were made were in 1926 and 1936. In 1926 Sir Henry Drayton, I believe then acting leader of the opposition, made a motion very similar to that which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) is making to-day. It was for a return of all orders in council passed in the current year 1925. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) at that time said, in reply to the request:	.
I would ask my hon. friend if he really desires all that he is requesting here. As my hon. friend knows, there are a great many orders in council that are purely routine orders, having to do with regulations, promotions, transfers of land, property and so forth, and to bring down all that is asked for here I am afraid would mean a very large and quite unnecessary expense. If my hon. friend would indicate the orders he has in mind there would be no objection.
There was some discussion at that time, and if Hansard is consulted it will be seen that the Prime Minister indicated to Sir Henry Drayton that if he. would attend at the office of the clerk of the privy council the index of the orders in council would be made available to him and he might indicate the orders in which he was interested. There is no disposition at all to withhold any orders, if some selection is made in accordance with the subjects in which the opposition is interested. In this case, however, the great mass of treasury board minutes and other decisions, as well as the orders in council, I am told would entail the employment of at least six stenographers, and that it would be two months before the copies of these orders in council and treasury board minutes could be made.
The second occasion was in 1936, when Mr. Bennett, then leader of the opposition, moved the following motion:
For a copy of all orders in council passed since the 23rd day of October. 1935. excepting appendices and treasury board minutes and excepting orders already tabled.
The discussion will be found in Hansard of March 23, 1936. That was a much more limited motion than the one we are now considering, but the Prime Minister took exception to it and the motion was negatived, 
apparently not on division, after some discussion in the house between the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition.
I do not know that I can say much more about the matter except that as acting Prime Minister I would not like to have a new precedent created for the blanket production of all orders in council covering a certain period. Rather I should prefer to have the effort made that was made in 1926 and again in 1936. If the leader of the opposition will himself go or designate somebody to go and look at the index of orders in council, make a selection and then make a motion covering the matters which are really of importance or of interest to the opposition, every effort will be made to meet their desires. It is rather hard to explain what a great number of very small matters indeed are covered by orders in council, relating to a vast multiplicity of details.
As I have said already, I would not like to consent, nor do I think I can consent, as acting Prime Minister, in the absence of the Prime Minister, to the creation of a precedent here which would be something entirely new in this or any. other parliamentary assembly. I am willing to let the motion stand and have the hon. gentleman consider what I have said, or I would ask him to withdraw the motion and adopt the course I have indicated. If that is not agreeable to him, however, I am afraid I will have to take the position that we cannot agree to the motion.

speechtext:
Thank you very much,
Mr. Speaker. When you rose I was afraid you were going to deny me the privilege you had allowed the leader of the government, in which case of course I should have had to object.
The acting Prime Minister has objected to the adoption of this motion on three grounds, as I understand his remarks he says that it will establish a precedent which has never been followed before and that a similar motion was moved on two occasions and for various

Orders in Council Minutes
reasons not passed. He instanced one occasion in 1926 when a whole year's orders in council were asked for. and another in 1936 when orders in council covering a period of six months were sought. He objects to the present motion on the ground that it establishes a precedent.
Then he objects on the ground that it does not ask for specific orders in council. It does not. I shall deal with that later. But I may say here and now that, with regard to treasury minutes, I have no objection at all to this house omitting them from the motion, if that will help us to make progress with the passage of the motion.
The third ground of objection was that of costs. The minister says that it might take six stenographers a period of two months to do the work required.
I had hoped the government might accept this motion, but I was aware that on one or two previous occasions motions of a similar type, but of a much wider extent, had been denied. Since the acting leader of the government has been allowed to state his case, I should like to state mine briefly, and I hope I can do so in five minutes.
I placed the motion on the order paper for a definite and very important purpose. It is a vital principle, which no member will dare to challenge, that this House of Commons has the full and inalienable right to a disclosure of all actions of the executive. It has the right and the duty to review and pass upon all such actions. Except in some minor matters where the king's prerogative has not been abridged, the executive or cabinet acts properly only under authority delegated by this parliament. Thus, in order that we may be aware of the actions of the executiye, I have placed this motion on the order paper.
This is not a fishing expedition. We think that, as representatives of the people, we ought to know what is going on. Under these various statutes power is given the government to pass orders in council. In a return tabled a little while ago the government let us know that sixty odd thousand orders in council and sixty odd thousand treasury minutes had been passed in the last six years. We think we ought to know the substance of those orders in council. I would repeat that this is not a fishing expedition. As representatives of the people we wish to know and we have the right to know what the government does by order in council.
If this high court of parliament is unaware of all the actions of the executive, not only is it deprived of its rights, but it is placed in a position where it cannot adequately carry out its solemn and responsible duties.
This is not an idle gesture on my part. I am not seeking any general warrant to search the files of the privy council to discover something which might be of political advantage.
I am seeking to restore to this house a right and a duty which it must possess and carry out if our representatitve institutions are to survive. For so long as I hold this seat I am determined to ensure, in so far as lies within my power, that Canada is governed by this House of Commons, by the elected representatives of the Canadian people, and not by the secret diplomacy of the council chamber. That, Mr. Speaker, I repeat is my motive in placing this motion on the order paper.
The greatest virtue of democracy is that it is conducted publicly, under the full scrutiny of the people. During war years we submitted to what amounted practically to cabinet dictatorship. Surely there can be no grounds for parliament's not knowing what that dictatorship did.
In many acts of parliament there are sections which require that all orders in council passed pursuant to those acts shall be laid on the table within a specified period of time. In some cases parliament has neglected to make such a provision. But that fact certainly should not be taken as a reason for refusing to table orders in council.
The acting leader of the government has hinted that if I would ask for specific orders in council they would be tabled. That does not meet the situation at all. I have no means of knowing what orders in council have been passed under the different authorizing acts. No member of parliament, other than a cabinet minister, can have that knowledge.
Does the acting leader of the government suggest that we must go on fishing expeditions into different government departments to gain information which ought to be available to parliament and to the public, at least upon request? Does he mean to suggest that such a course should be adopted, when he knows as well as I do that we have not only the right but the duty to review all these orders in council, and when he knows perfectly well that we have no means of knowing how many or of what character these orders in council are?
We can guess the character of some of them. One was tabled the other day, only after the press had learned about it somewhere. Some others were tabled as a result of an order of the house passed on a motion moved by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker). Among other things, sessional paper 188, dated October 22, had this to say-and we were not on a fishing expedition then either, but when this kind of thing comes out I think we ought to have the privilege of seeing all

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext:
I say that is not the proper way or place to make provisions of that kind.
As I said, there are numerous examples of parliament's learning of important orders in council long after such orders have been passed. Let us take only one example. On May 7, 1945, a very important order in council was passed dealing with Eldorado mines, and an amending order on September 5. When did parliament learn about these orders in council? Not until October 25, just a few days ago, five or six months after the first of those orders in council was passed. And even then we learned of it only after the press had discovered it, and the government only then thought it wise to table the order in council in the house.
In this motion I have limited my request to orders in council passed since September 6, 1945, the date upon which this parliament assembled less than eight weeks ago. My reason is that I believe it to be of particular importance for us to know to what extent the government is acting by order in council, at a time when the house is in session, in respect of questions about which we should have knowledge. I repeat that the house is entitled to have the substance of all orders in council.
The minister who has just spoken, the acting leader of the 'government, has. quoted precedents which he alleges uphold the position

he takes. I say that you cannot use precedents as an argument for meeting unprecedented situations. It is an unprecedented situation when under the War Measures Act and other measures 90,000 orders in eouneil and treasury minutes have been passed in a period of six years and are even now being passed, as the minister says, at a rate which will necessitate six stenographers working for two months to copy what have been passed in the last eight weeks.
I am not interested in maintaining bad precedents. If parliament made a mistake in years gone by, no matter who was the prime minister or what party was in power, now is the time and the opportunity to improve such procedure. The acting leader of the government has raised the question of the cost of obtaining the material I have requested. Surely this argument is not advanced seriously when this government is now spending $14,000,000 a day, or $5,000,000,000 this year. Surely the argument that it will require half a dozen stenographers working for two months is not advanced seriouslj'. What cost is entailed in having an extra copy of every order in council made at the time it is approved and held in readiness to be laid on the table of the house at the appropriate time?
I strongly urge the government to reconsider the stand it has taken. It is inconceivable that the government will deny to the people's representatives the knowledge which is required if this house is to perform its duty. If the government refuses this request, my only course is to submit the motion to the judgment of the house. I appeal to all hon. members, wherever they may sit, to join with me in asserting and establishing a vital principle, a principle without which we cannot have responsible government. To hon. members who sit to your right I make a particular appeal. The fate of the government is not at stake in this motion. Let us join together in this instance in asserting the rights of parliament and the rights of the peoples' representatives in order to avoid leaving the government open to the charge that it is either a dictatorship or a bureaucracy or an oligarchy rather than the thoroughly representative and responsible institution which it ought to be and which the Canadian people want it to be.

The hon. member for Lincoln, and perhaps some others, asked me to give the figures on N.R.M.A. personnel discharged during 1945. These figures by months are as follows: January, 536; February, 450; March, 461; April, 494; May, 588; June, 615; July, 969; August, 1,774; September, 2,942; October, up to the 27th, 2,332, making a total up to October 27 of 11,161. The committee will note that up to the end of May the total was 2,529, and from June 1 to October 27, the total was 8,632. The breakdown, by cause, of discharge of the 8,632 since June 1 is as follows: On compassionate grounds, in which is included those previously out on compassionate or other farm leave, 4,911. That figure includes 2,727 men who were on such leave prior to V-E day. That is the first group. On medical grounds, 2,736; demobilization of those under the age of nineteen, 542; those released to engage in work of national importance, 216; and other grounds, including misconduct, 227.

The hon-. member for Swift Current drew attention to the large proportion of commission ranks granted to the men from the various districts. I have not checked his figures, but I have no doubt that the proportions which he has calculated are correct; but they do not indicate any intent on anyone's part to grant commissions to men from one district and to withhold them from men of other districts. I can assure my hon. friend that there never has been any such policy, and the basis of granting promotions or commissions has been on merit. He drew attention to the large proportion of officers from military district 4, my own district. I have no particular explanation to offer for that, other than to suggest that perhaps it is accounted for by the fact that from this district, in which we have the largest city in Canada, a very large proportion of medical and dental officers would have been drawn, and that might well account for the somewhat large proportion of officer personnel. He also drew attention to the proportion of officers among those enlisted outside Canada. That proportion is high, but I am advised that the numbers are comparatively small, and the reason suggested is that, although we did not enlist many men- outside Canada, we did grant commissions to a certain number of specialist personnel in the United Kingdom, and some of those commissions went to Canadian residents there.

The approximate number of United States military forces in Canada as at this date is as folloyvs: in northwest Canada, engaged in air staging, maintenance, handling of stores, disposal of property, airfields Edmonton to Alaska, Canal project, Alaska highway, Yukon-Whitehorse railway, 3,193; in northeast Canada excluding Labrador, engaged mainly in staging and caretaking of airfields and weather stations, 360; at Prince Rupert, a sub-port of embarkation which is to be de-activated as soon as possible, 610. The hon. gentleman also asked whether it is contemplated that a plan of cadet training of public and high school students will be carried out. Then he asked whether all Canadian prisoners of war have been returned to Canada or, if not, what the reason was for any delay.
I am advised that at the present time there are two prisoners of war from Hong Kong not yet back in Canada but that both these men. are en route to this country. As at October 10, 1945, there were 615 liberated prisoners of war still in the United Kingdom or on the continent. As the committee knows, liberated prisoners of war are eligible for special priority return to Canada if they have 47696-107
been six months or more in enemy hands or if they have been less than six months in enemy hands and have served overseas for three years or more. Of the 615 to whom I have referred, 565 are not eligible for special priority return; 42 are eligible for special priority return but have preferred to remain in the United Kingdom for personal reasons. In addition, there was one man in hospital; there were three deserters and four in penal servitude.
The final question the hon. gentleman asked was how many enemy prisoners of war there are in Canada at the present time; how many have been returned to Germany or Italy, and whether any arrangements were likely to be made for securing payment from enemy countries for the cost of maintenance of these prisoners. As the committee knows, the great majority of the prisoners of war in Canada are held by us for the account of the British government. There are at the present time about 34,000 enemy prisoners of war in Canada. Not one has been returned to his homeland since V-E day. Some small numbers were repatriated under the terms of the Geneva convention. That was done prior to V-E day, but at the moment I have not the figure available.
Then, the matter of securing payment for the cost of maintenance of those prisoners does not come under my department. I suggest that the question might be directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, when his estimates are under consideration.
I believe I have covered most of the questions asked during yesterday's debate. There was one question respecting the cost of N.R.M.A. personnel, concerning which I am obtaining information. I shall put it on record at a later date.

Mr. D1EFENBAKER: The minister said this afternoon that a Canadian court-martial was being set up, or probably I should call it a Canadian military court, to try General Meyer. I believe there will be general commendation of that move. As a matter of fact one point which has impressed me in connection with the set-up of the international military tribunal designed for the purpose, of trying war criminals is that there has been no Canadian representative on that tribunal. Many have felt that, in view of the fact that Canadians were murdered as a result of orders given by this general, or by SS troops under bis command, he should be tried before a Canadian court in order to carry out the promise and pledge of this parliament that hose who committed such wrongs would be aunished.
That brings me to another point, and that is that only two of the men still remain in Hong Kong. Coming to Ottawa recently on the train, I met with members of the armed forces who had been prisoners at Hong Kong. The stories they told about the cruelties and atrocities were such as to demand certain punishment of the perpetrators of those crimes. I should like to hear from the minister a statement as to whether or not a Canadian tribunal will be set up for the purpose of trying Japanese captors who committed unexampled crimes and offences against Canadians. It might be said that any court could try them; but I feel that the court which tries the perpetrators of the crimes against Hong Kong prisoners should be one constituted by Canada.
I come now to a discussion of the whole situation in connection with court-martial sentences on Canadians overseas. According to a return brought down in answer to certain questions I asked, up to September 1 there were 2,776 Canadians sentenced to periods of from one to three years, and 302 to periods over three years. There is provision in King's regulations and orders (Canada), as it now stands, for appeals against these sentences. But in the very nature of things those appeals cannot be as complete as would be appeals to judicial bodies. While there is opportunity to appeal either to a senior military authority, or directly to the governor in council, I believe that something should be done toward setting up a judicial tribunal to overhaul these sentences.

I realize that steps are being taken in that direction at the present time. I suggest, however, that immediate steps should be taken so that the Department of Justice could be consulted. As I read paragraph 574, the Department of Justice could be given the immediate opportunity of looking into these sentences in order to assure that no injustices will have been done. I refer to offences other than criminal, or to military offences as such which, during the period of the war, in the interests of discipline required exemplary sentences.
All hon. members recognize that such sentences were necessary, but with the restoration of peace I am sure most hon. members have had brought to their attention cases which would lead them to believe that everything should be done toward the amelioration of those sentences. I am not here to attack court-martial justice, but I will say that the rights of accused persons are not as fully assured in those courts-martial as they would have been in civil courts of law. I ask for a reconsideration of sentences imposed-and at once.
I find that some 958 sentences have been varied. Would the minister advise the committee as to the number of sentences reversed on appeal, first by the governor in council or, second, by a superior military authority?
All hon. members have had brought to their attention cases respecting young men who have served from one and a half to two years in the front line and who then, for some reason which they cannot explain, have deserted. Some were, away for only a few hours, and others for a few days. I have in mind particularly one young man who was wounded in the hip and as a [DOT] result was in hospital for a period of time. Finally shrapnel was removed. When a shortage of reinforcements made necessary the gathering together in Italy of many men for the attack on the Gothic line, he was mobilized back into the front line, but said that he could not go. He had given two years service. I believe that young man went overseas before he had reached eighteen years, simply by advancing his age-and the minister knows that is often done.	-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have done it.

I know. That
young man had served honourably, but he is now serving a sentence of three years in the penitentiary.
These men are being brought back to Canada to serve their sentences. I have in mind one boy from Regina who was sentenced to four years less eighteen months. He was

Demobilization-Army
taken from his original place of incarceration and returned to Canada. While on board ship he did orderly work, and was as free as could be. Upon arrival in Regina the military police said to him, "You are going to be taken into custody to serve the remainder of your sentence." He was sent to Prince Albert penitentiary where he will have to associate, not with men who committed offences against military law, but with hardened criminals.
Surely the time has come when something should be done to relieve this condition, having in mind the facilities and institutions available in Canada. These men who are required to serve sentences for other than criminal offences should not be placed in penal institutions where they will be in touch with hardened criminals and, in many instances, influenced to follow lives of crime.
I have spoken to penitentiary guards and, without exception, they % are shocked when they have to treat these young men as criminals. They ask that something be done. I am not thinking of those who were charged with treason or with criminal offences of violence; I am thinking of those who in the hour of stress and by reason of a lack, we will say, of moral stamina, men who perhaps had no control, committed these offences and are now serving these sentences.
In the interests of fairness and of justice, above all in the interests of the parents of these boys and their loved ones, I ask the minister to see that these sentences are reviewed immediately. This should not be done by one man set up as a judicial committee; a sufficient number of judges should be assigned to this work to ensure immediate consideration of the matter. If not judges, then trained! officials of the Department of Justice should be assigned. In the course of my practice I have had many occasions to bring matters to the attention of the Department of Justice with a view to obtaining pardons or paroles, and I have found that the permanent officials give to the consideration of each case a personal attention that is most commendable and assures certain justice.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I am glad the hon. member for Lake Centre has brought up this matter of reviewing sentences of this kind. About a month ago I took steps, on the advice of the officers of the department, to see that such a review was made. I have not made any public announcement that this step had been taken, because I did not think it particularly desirable that we should make a press statement about the setting up of a board of review.
47696-107J
We have created a special review board of which Mr. Justice Iveiller Mackay is the chairman. The other two members are Major General Tremblay and Brigadier Nolan. Hon. members will know who Brigadier Nolan is. I think it is a first-class board. That board is reviewing sentences that are considered to be longer than usual, cases such as my hon. friend has referred' to where a man has been sentenced to one, two, three, four or five years, for either a military offence or a civilian offence. This is in addition to the regular means of appeal with which the committee is familiar, and with which the hon. member for Lake Centre is particularly familiar, that is, the appeal to the minister or to the governor in council.
The board will proceed on the assumption that the proceedings were regular and that the sentence was proper, taking into account military law and all the circumstances. They are reviewing the whole proceedings to see whether each case is one in which clemency should be exercised. In other words, the board is intended in large measure to perform the functions which the remission branch of the Department of Justice performs with respect to civilian offences.

Will they all be
reviewed, or just those that are brought to the attention of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Not every sentence; it is only those cases in which the sentence is over a certain period.
Would the minister like me to bring to his attention a case in which a five-year sentence was imposed?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The hon. member may bring it to my attention if he wishes, but any sentences of five years would be automatically reviewed by the board. I am advised that all sentences to penitentiaries are being reviewed.
How many of the men are actually in the Canadian penitentiaries?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I will have to take note
of that question and get the information, because it is not before me at the moment. I really did not mean ito interrupt the hon. member for Lake Centre, but I thought that it was perhaps a good time to make a statement to the committee. I have explained why I did not- make an earlier announcement about the appointment of this special reviewing committee. It is performing what I think is a very necessary function, but it was not one that I felt needed to be advertised.

I should like to say something on this point, something which the hon. member for Lake Centre did not mention.
