speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Lake Centre has the floor.
The minister had the floor.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Lake Centre had the floor. He asked one question which the minister answered. If the hon. member for Lake Centre wishes to continue, he may do so.
I have been sitting here for about five weeks listening to this discussion, and I merely wanted to ask one question.

We have both
been sitters. I have not been asking any questions, and I just wanted to finish this up.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I was wondering when the
hon. member was going to start.

As a matter of
fact there have been so many good questions asked that I could not find any others to ask. However, I was not satisfied with some of the answers. The personnel of the board speaks well for the board. About the middle of June I brought up the question of the sentences which had been imposed in connection with the Halifax trouble, and I also referred to court martial sentences. I am sure the personnel of this appeal board will commend itself to all. However, one judge and two military officers sitting to consider 3,000 cases means that not many cases will be heard.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
They are being disposed
of very rapidly.

In the case of the
army there have been 300 sentences of over three years, and I could hardly believe that these could be decided very rapidly. Possibly the minister could tell us how many sentences have so far been reviewed by this semi-judicial board, and in how many cases have there been remissions or variations or reduction.
There is another matter which naturally arises, and which has not yet been dealt with; I refer to absentees and deserters. On October 5, 1945, an answer to a question I had asked indicated that 11,145 N.R.M.A. men were deserters or absentees, and that there were 13,416 draft dodgers. I asked how many had been prosecuted for desertion and, if my memory serves me aright, the answer was that there were no figures on that. No doubt those figures will now be available.
As I understand the situation, when reference was made to desertions which first took place in December, 1944, and January, 1945, the then minister of national defence said that in the case of those who had deserted
[Mr. Gillia.)
after being ordered overseas, proceedings would be taken at the expiry of twenty-eight days. I have his statement here, but I do not think there is any question that he made that statement on February 2, 1945. As I understand the situation, if the prosecution for being absent without leave takes place before the commanding officer, the maximum sentence that can be imposed is twenty-eight days. But if the man is taken before a court marital, wide powers rest in the court-martial authority. As a matter of fact press reports in various -parts of the country indicate that sentences running from twelve to eighteen months have been imposed. I am sure that the minister is as desirous as anybody else to ensure that there should be uniformity of sentences for this offence, just as appeal courts in respect of the criminal law endeavour to secure uniformity of sentence, making due allowance for conditions and extenuating circumstances in individual cases.
My questions therefore to the minister are these: How many prosecutions have taken place for desertion of deserters from the N.R.M.A.? How many of these prosecutions have been by court martial, and how many by trial before the commanding officer? I should also like to have a break-down by provinces of the number of court-martial trials for this offence. I am sure that the desire of the department, just as in setting up this committee under Mr. Justice Keiller Mackay, who is a great soldier and a distinguished jurist, will be to secure toleration, fairness and equality in sentences and a measure of justice that cannot be secured when sentences may be determined by individuals without regard for uniformity,
I would ask the minister to advise the committee with regard to this subject, which is a vexed one, but one that will have to be faced in the interests of fairness and justice. If it is not faced, and if we in this parliament take the stand, let bygones be bygones; a general amnesty is the easy solution, we put the stamp of approbation on crime committed during a period of war and at the same time penalize those who answered their country's call and when directed overseas went overseas regardless of consequences to themselves.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I presume that my hon. friend will be satisfied with the statistics by military districts. We do not keep them by provinces.
Yes.

Mr. Chairman, I had not intended taking part in the general discussion, but I was rather waiting for specific items to be called. But this discussion is

Demobilization-Army
likely to be a general one for some considerable time, and to break the monotony of having it all come from one corner of the chamber I might as well join in.
The hon. member for Lake Centre has raised a question that to me is particularly interesting, the review of court-martial sentences. But he missed one point upon which I was waiting with great interest to hear him comment 'as a legal man. Last June a considerable number of these cases came to my attention, and I was amazed to find at that itime that several service personnel with three and a half to four years' service overseas were being returned to their district depots, discharged in the district depots and sent to civilian prisons. I thought that there must be a mistake somewhere, and so I took it upon myself to write the Minister of Justice and the Department of National Defence and ask if a soldier convicted of a military offence could legally be confined to a civilian prison. Up to to-day I have not yet received an official decision from either source on that point. I do not know myself just what the legal position is, but it does not seem right to me. I think that before the minister finishes with his estimates he should state definitely that this question is being worked out between Justice and National Defence departments. They may be able to legalize the incarceration of a soldier in a civilian prison because of a military offence; nevertheless that is not justice. I shall be interested to hear from the minister on that point.
Another serious aspect of the matter is that a number of these boys are married; they have wife and children. When they are discharged from the service their pay and allowances ceases, and to-diay many women and children in this country are objects of charity because their husbands who saw' fit to defend this country in her hour of need are now' languishing as convicts in a civilian prison. Immediate steps should be taken by the Department of National Defence to make some provision for the wife, and family of a soldier who finds himself in that position.
I am not going to say anything about the point score system, because I think that discussion is six months too late. The time is past for it. We have discussed it in the house for the last four years and expressed strong opinions on the subject and made recommendations with regard to rehabilitation and all the rest of it. A lot of our recommendations were not carried out. But it is too late now to start making changes in the scheme of repatriation, because most of the boys are back or are on their way back. A lot of boys from the different divisions are writing
me that they are coming home, and the boys in the third division write me that they expect to be back in November. So I am not going to say anything about that.
With regard to the army of occupation, it was the consensus of this house that any army of occupation that we raised to make our proper contribution in Europe until such time as the peoples there can look after themselves w'ould be raised on a voluntary basis, and I was amazed to hear that men with long periods of service overseas are being practically conscripted and retained1 in the army of occupation-.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: They cannot be sent back until their turn comes. They are bound to be doing something over there.

You are raising an army of
25,000	to remain- over there indefinitely?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have not said how long they would remain. I madie an extended statement on that yesterday.
They will remain until Germany and Europe are in a position to look after themselves.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That remains to be seen.
There is no sense in quibbling over it. I visualize their being there for the next four or five years.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I hope you are wrong.

I hope I am too, but I do not think I am. The army of occupation should be raised on a voluntary basis. I do not think anyone should be taken by the neck at this stage of the game, particularly men w'ho went through the war, and be told: You are going to remain in Europe whether you like it or not. We have an army in Canada, and I am sure that there are a lot of'boys-in this country who would be glad- to go over and join the army of occupation. I realize that there may be certain service personnel who must be retained there because of the exigencies of the service. That is a good excuse under all circumstances. That is all I am going to say on that.
With respect to this board of review that is being set up to review court-martial cases, I am not satisfied with the minister's statement. We set up a board, and I think he was wrong in not announcing it because many of us who have been writing to his department for a number of months past have been quite anxious about a review of the whole matter. In my opinion he should have publicized it because it was a move in the right direction. I would understand from his statement that
Demobilization-Army

the review of these cases from one year up to three years is automatic; the board examines into them whether the cases are referred to it or appealed or otherwise. The idea is to bring uniformity into the sentences.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is not that. It is performing very much the functions that the remissions branch of the Department of Justice carries out. It reviews cases on the assumption that there was a fair trial and that the sentence was one which was properly awarded. They look into the cases, however, to see whether in the circumstances clemency should be exercised, especially perhaps with respect to offences which, as the hon. member for Lake Centre said, were purely military, the time having come when they should be reconsidered. While the war is on, the military. courts may have to impose severe sentences for what is technical desertion in the face of the enemy, but after the war is over these sentences should possibly be pretty carefully reviewed to see whether the time has come for the exercise of clemency, and that is one of the things the board will do.

But it is automatic. One
does not have to hire a lawyer.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
No. It is entirely within
the department, and that is one reason why I gave no particular publicity to it, I did not want the board subjected to a whole lot of requests and submissions from outside even at the instance of members of my own profession.
I hope it is not just another board but one that will do something.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is working hard.

I have been writing to the
department for a considerable time in reference to some of these cases and nothing has been done about them. If the board has been working hard it has not touched any of the problems with which I have been concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
They started about three
weeks or a month ago.
They are probably just finding out where the files are.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That preparatory work was all done ahead of time.

I will not criticize them until I find out what they are doing, but I am interested in this point. While the board may draw, from the man's file,, a skeleton sketch of the evidence, it will not have before it in the file many facts which the man would be able to give the board himself if he appeared before it or if he were represented. I am wondering if it is possible to give the Canadian Legion,
	,
for example, or the army and navy veterans, the right to have a representative on the board. Then, if a case is coming up where a soldier desires to have representation, the representative from the veterans' organizations can make a presentation of the facts on his behalf, those facts being set out by the soldier himself. I have had the privilege of appearing before .many boards to represent soldiers, and I know that in many cases the soldier who was present just sat there and would have been in a bad spot many times if he did not have someone with a little more gall than himself to get up and try to unravel the problem for him. The soldier should have the right of representation. Juggling with a man's future is a serious business, particularly when misconduct discharge and all that sort of thing is involved, and whether he is placed in that position or not is a matter that should be carefully considered. I think the board that is now being set up should make reasonably sure of all the facts in any case that comes before it to see that those facts are properly presented in order that it may make a proper decision and not one that is based simply on an outline taken from the files, because files are very often far from complete.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Pretty complete, the ones I have looked over.

I have seen court-martial proceedings-I have copies of some of them- and if I were a magistrate I would want more evidence before me on which to convict anybody. I would ask the minister to consider the question of a representative from the veterans' organizations. Most of these men are qualified and sensible men. and they have a contribution to make to the board. .
I do not like to take up with the minister questions on which he cannot take some action, but I wish to discuss another problem with him and it is a specific one. It has to do with a case in connection with which I have been dealing with the department for the last year. It started in October. 1944. and ray last correspondence with the department was in October, 1945. I canvassed all the machinery of his department. I wish the minister would talk to his officials about this case. The number is F.332213, Locke. This boy in the first place enlisted in the air force and went to Toronto where he was taking training, and then they decided to cut down the air force and he was called into the army. At the time he was called into the army' he was serving in Toronto with the air force and they decided to let him out. They gave him transportation back to his home, and he was called for the army in M.D. No. 6. He was discharged from the air force on February

Deinobilization-Army
9,	1944, according to the certificate which I have here and which the minister's department has had for some time. He signed that certificate on February 9, 1944, in Toronto, but it was not confirmed until April 14, 1944, by the officer in charge of the station. He was issued transportation to his home in Glace Bay, Nova Scotia, which is 300 miles east of Halifax where the military district is located. The army officials mailed transportation to him from Halifax on the 1st of April, 1944. At the time the transportation was mailed to him he was in Toronto in the air force and yet they were calling him into the army. He did not receive his discharge certificate until March 3, 1945. That was his discharge from the air force. There was considerable neglect there in issuing that certificate because he signed it himself on February 9, 1944, and, as I say, he did not receive it until March 3, 1945. In the meantime he had waited at his home four months for that discharge from the air force and was waiting for transportation to M.D. No. 6 in Halifax. In the interval he could not secure employment. He reported to the selective service people, and he went to the military authorities in Sydney, Nova Scotia, with his pack to go back to Halifax to join the army. They said, "There is no transportation; you go home and wait". He waited for four months and the selective service could not give him interim employment because he had no discharge certificate. Meanwhile his father began to write to the military authorities asking them to reimburse him for board at $10 a week for this boy who was waiting at home to go into the army and could not get employment because he had no discharge certificate. . The boy in the meantime went into the service and proceeded overseas, and during most of the time this correspondence hgs been going on between the air force, the army and myself and the boy's father he has been there. He is in Holland at the present time. The claim is for four months' board of the boy during the time in which he could not get employment because someone made a mistake in not getting out the certificate.
In the first place I took the matter up with the air force and they made a definite decision in regard to it. In a long letter dated March 14, 1945, the air force advised me on the matter. They said that the responsibility was the army's. The letter was signed by T. C. Thompson, group captain or secretary. This is what he said:	*
It appears that the discharge certificate was misplaced by the military authorities and was not passed to this ex-airman. It has been recovered through the officer in charge of records, Department of National Defence, Army at Ottawa, and dispatched to the ex-airman.
Evidently it was in Ottawa. The air force definitely placed this matter on the army. I then began to take it up with the army, and I have quite a lot of correspondence here. I am not going to read it all, but the minister can check the file, which will be a duplicate of what I have here. In the last letter I received, dated October 19, 1945, they definitely ruled this out as a claim. They say that they are not accepting any responsibility; that there is no provision for payment of a claim of this kind, and all that sort of thing. The facts of the matter are that this man bills the Department of, National Defence, Army, for $160 board for the son during the period when he was sitting at home waiting for a call to go in. Because he had no discharge certificate he could not get employment. That responsibility belongs to the army. Even if they have to add it to the national debt they should pay it because I believe it is their legitimate responsibility. I ask the minister to check on the matter personally, because I have done everything I can with the officials of his department in the past year. There are several things that I am going to take up when the specific items are before us, but I wanted to bring this to the minister's attention at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall certainly look at the file. It is a very interesting story. I shall give a little gratuitous advice. I might suggest that the young man hire a good lawyer; he will have to be a good one though. After listening to the recital of facts, and expressing a free opinion myself I would say there is no claim.
No claim?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No claim.
If they hired a lawyer and obtained the $160 they would wind up broke.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I make no comment on that.
I now- have the figures with respect to the break-down of those N.R.M.A. personnel on extended leave as of October 15. They are as follows: Compassionate farm leave 4,705; hog and dairy leave 119; spring and harvest leave 77; industrial leave, 3,340; compassionate leave, 716; logging and forestry leave, 108; coal mining leave, 483; other leave, 27; total, 9,575.
Before we leave this question of desertion I should like to get some information from the minister. He spoke about the board of appeal-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

speechtext: I suppose that this board of review will review cases of desertion as well as other cases. The reason I bring this to the attention of the minister at this time is that in the past I have had correspondence with the minister's department in regard to ca^es of desertion. I have one man particularly in mind. I am not going to review the case because it is now with the department. No decision has been reached other than to say that if this prisoner has good conduct he may get one-third of his sentence remitted. I have had information that in some cases' these sentences are cut by one-half of the time for good behaviour. Within the last couple of days I have received two letters from parents whose boys have been sentenced for desertion. The thing that is bothering them is a statement which appeared in the press not long ago with regard to men who are deserters and are now reporting in the province of Quebec and who are supposed-and I use the word advisedly-to be let out after twenty-eight days detention.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is completely inaccurate.

I was not going to bring this question up, but as the parents have been in touch with me personally, on one occasion by telegram and on two other occasions by airmail, I thought the minister should make some statement in regard to it, because it is causing a great deal of hard feeling to parents in western Canada whose boys have been convicted on charges of desertion and whose sentences are running,, in the two cases I have in mind, from twelve to eighteen months. When they see some who have been away as deserters for a very long time and who are now reporting, according to the press, and serving only twenty-eight days, it can be well imagined that there will be a lot of trouble if this difficulty is not solved. I hope that the minister is in a position to make a statement now for the benefit of the parents of those boys who have received long sentences for desertion.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
It may be as well for me to make the statement now. I thought I might cover the whole question when I gave the statistical data for which the hon. member for Lake Centre asked. I saw the report in the press of alleged promises made to deserters if they reported. In view of the circumstances under which it was made, I assumed that it related to M.D. No. 5 with headquarters in Quebec. I asked for a report as to what the real situation was, because the statement which appeared in the press did not coincide with the information I had been getting, and complaints I had been receiving from members and others in the province of Quebec that the sentences which were being awarded were far too heavy, particularly for farm workers and the like. Sentences of eighteen months to two years were being awarded and they thought that was far too much.
As I say, I asked for a report from the district officer commanding M.D. No. 5. I am advised that there is no record of any such promise having been made. I may say, in addition, that I spoke to-day to the colonel who commands the district depot in Quebec, who assures me that that is quite correct, that no such promise has been made and that as a matter iof fact virtually all these cases were being tried by court martial and fairly substantial sentences were being awarded. The impression as to these twenty-eight day sentences may have been created by instructions which were sent out to all district officers commanding and to the district officer commanding Pacific command on February 12, 1945. I shall not read the whole signal which was sent out, as I say, to all district officers commanding, but I shall read one paragraph, which is as follows:
Having in mind the foregoing, and with due regard to the responsibility of the district officer commanding for the administration of discipline within his district, it is considered that in dealing with offences of absenteeism and desertion in cases where the offender's conduct has not in the past been bad, and where the offender has voluntarily surrendered, the case should normally be dealt with by the commander summarily as a case of absence without leave, in order that the offender may be dispatched overseas with an early draft.
The committee will recall that at that time the major number of desertions were those of personnel who had been notified to. proceed overseas on a draft. It was felt that since the purpose of desertion was bo avoid going overseas to serve, that purpose would be achieved if the offender were tried by court martial here and sentenced to a period of detention in Canada. Therefore it was decided that the district officers commanding should use their discretion, of course, and try these cases summarily.

Demobilization-Army
What was the date of that order?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
As I mentioned a moment ago, it was February 12, 1945. That went out to all district officers commanding. On July 26 a general signal or general order, or whatever it is called, was sent out to the same people, the district officers commanding and the G.O.C. of the Pacific command, part of which I will read. The first paragraph was:
1. On 12 February, 1945, in view of the fact that there was an urgent need for dispatch of troops overseas, and that the incidence of absenteeism might be due to the desire to avoid overseas dispatch, instructions were conveyed to you by telegram Rank 3435 that in dealing with absentees and deserters whose conduct had not been bad and where the offender had voluntarily surrendered, the case should normally be d' alt with by the commander summarily as a case of absence without leave in order that the offender might be dispatched overseas with an early draft and so defeat the purpose of the offence of absenteeism.
Then it goes on to say that the cessation, of host ilities in Europe has radically changed the situation in this regard, and so on. Then I read paragraph 5:
5.	. . the urgent situation which gave rise to the dispatch of telegram Rank 3435 has now ceased to exist, and it is considered that the normal practice of dealing with the offences of desertion and of absence without leave should obtain in the future.
6.	The foregoing is intended for your general guidance and for discussion by you with commanding officers within your command,
7.	This must not be taken as inferring that sentenees for desertion are at present too severe. In fact, it is possible that the handling of cases of desertion has been too lenient in the light of the seriousness of the offence.
8.	These remarks must not be taken as indicating in any way that in the review of sentences, suspension or remission should not be freely exercised at the earliest possible moment after it is considered that the interests of discipline have been served.
As a good many hon. members of the committee know, every sentence for desertion or anything else is reviewed on the expiration of forty-five days, if it is for ninety days or more; and it is reviewed periodically. Ordinarily one-third of the sentence is taken off for good conduct, and I believe that in a good many cases the average sentence served for offences of that kind is about half the sentence originally imposed. The general practice, I am advised-and this prevails in the province of Quebec as well as elsewhere-is that the sentence approximates the period during which the offender has been absent without leave or has deserted. As the committee understands the D.O.C. has the power to remit. In a certain number of cases men were out on farm leave at V-E day, and this applies in all 47696-108
provinces. A good many of them just did not come back after V-E day when their leave was up; they thought the war was over and they could stay on the farm and it would be all right. Had they reported back in most cases, their leave would have been extended, but a good many of them just did not do so. After twenty-one days technically they became deserters and were listed as such. Some were picked up; others came in later voluntarily and surrendered. I am told that in a good many of these cases or at any rate in some of these cases the commanding officer has tried them summarily and has sentenced them to twenty-eight days' detention on the assumption that it was more a technical defect than anything else, that they would have had their farm leave extended but had not done so. In other cases where the sentence has been somewhat longer, the D.O.C. has remitted perhaps more than normally wmuld have been the case.
At my owm request I have had a report made as to the sentences awarded in different parts of Canada because, as the committee will appreciate, I have been getting a great many letters from hon. members on all sides of the house and from all parts of Canada on this question of sentences for absenteeism and desertion. The reports I have received indicate that the sentences in the province of Quebec are neither more lenient nor more severe than in the rest of Canada.
From what the minister has said I would take it that there is a good deal of truth in the statement reported in the press.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
No, I would say there is
very little truth in the statement as reported in the press. The statement I saw was that men were surrendering on the assurance or the promise that they would be given only twenty-eight days' detention. I am assured by the district officer commanding at M.D. No. 5 and by the officer commanding the depot at M.D. No. 5 that such is not the case.

It seems to me that the minister has been reviewing the general practice rather than the specific cases which were mentioned in the press. I can quite understand that boys who had been absent without leave for twenty-one days and who were charged with desertion might give themselves up on the word of a member of this house, say, as was reported in the press, that if they did so voluntarily they would be given only twenty-eight days' detention. They might not receive this assurance from the military authorities; I doubt if they would in cases

Demobilization-Army

like that, but if they have the assurance of some responsible person they would come and give themselves up voluntarily and be let out after twenty-eight days. I do not think there would be many such cases in western Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
There are not many in
the east, either.

Well, there would not
have to be very many to cause a great deal of dissatisfaction or to result in a great injustice being done those boys who are being given anywhere from twelve to eighteen months for practically the same offence. I think the minister should take more precautions, and certainly he should adopt some measures to see that the sentences throughout the whole country are more uniform.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: As I said before, I have investigated that situation and the sentences throughout the country are uniform. The complaints I am getting from the province of Quebec-and I am getting them every day- are that the sentences are too severe, that they are from twelve to fifteen or eighteen months or two years. That is the sort of complaint I am getting, I can assure my hon. friend; it is not that the sentences are too light.
The minister says he is getting those complaints, and I do not doubt his word; but is it the actual fact?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Yes, it is the fact; there is no question about that. I cannot emphasize it too strongly.
Mr. .CHURCH: I hesitate to enter this discussion, but coming from a city which has so many men left overseas I think it my duty to say something. I wish to compliment the minister on the courtesy lie show's here jn committee, and I should like to see his estimates go through, but in view of what has been said here in the last few days about the Toronto district I have a duty to perform. We have more soldiers left overseas than any other city in the dominion. We have been overlooked. Prior to the election, until June 11, nothing could be done. I have been complaining about this "first in, first out" system and the point ratio from the start. The point system is not a proper one. After every great war demobilization is the most complex and involved problem any government has to face. How are we facing it? I say to the minister that I believe in changing the system, and the sooner the better.
Hon. members know what the trouble is. How does it come about that Lieutenant General Crerar has been in Ottawa for nearly

two months, but has never been invited to come here and meet us and report to us. He is one of the world's best soldiers and could shed light on this question. If he had we might have avoided some of the debates we have had on this matter. He was not asked to come here at all and we have never met him. I have never seen him since his return, but he is an old friend of mine, and I paid tribute to him during discussions in the house in 1941-42 when he was being attacked unfairly here although, as I said, he needed no defence. He is getting the freedom of our city to-day.
I may say-and I am still of the same opinion-that he could have given us some light on this whole "first in, first out" rule and other problems. I make my appeal to the minister, who is a soldier himself, for the reasons I have given. Away back last July, after the. war with Germany, I tried to get certain information, but through all the months of May, June, July and August we in effect had no army minister and I could not get the information.
I wish to pay tribute to the permanent officials. I have never been one to attack them. They are, on the whole, a credit to the country. I know that Colonel A. Ross was good enough to reply to my correspondence. I think I have as much correspondence from soldiers overseas as any other member in the house and more, and I have gladly given more than half my days for six years to improve the lot of soldiers and their families.
The minister would be well advised to follow the advice I gave in a newspaper interview last July. Speaking to the Globe and Mail of July 17 I said:
The "first in, first out" rule, while correct in principle is not working out too well.
I pointed out that it would not work out well in actual practice, and would get worse after V-J day. What I have said has proven -to be true. As I look over the record, the situation is becoming more complex every day. We know the Prime* Minister went to the old country. One of the reasons he gave for going, in his first interview over there, was that of getting more information and to seek more shipping, so as to implement the "first in, first out" rule, and in that way to bring about some relief.
After all is said and done, changes should be made. I appeal to the present minister and his officials in this way: Do not be afraid to tell the people of Canada you have made a mistake. Canadians do not expect their leaders to be gods. Always tell the people

Demobilization-Army
the truth, and never legislate against human nature. Trust the people, and they will trust you.
I have been complaining for months before we met here about the complex system now in process of operation. I find- that soldiers are writing to me, young men, high school students who went overseas voluntarily. Now some of them are in Germany and they cannot get back. Some may have lost brothers over there. Fathers have gone away; youngest sons are over there and they cannot get back to school. The young man who enlisted at eighteen years of age would be twenty-seven years of age before he could start and finish a university course and become a dentist or a doctor or an electrical engineer.
I direct the minister's attention to the fact that changes will have to be made immediately. After the Crimean war the same trouble was experienced. Lord Salisbury said that one of the most common errors in politics [DOT] was sticking to the carcasses of diseased policies.
The policy the government has been offering has been weighed in the balance and found wanting. The defeat of Japan came so suddenly the point system fell down. A British white paper issued in September points out that the demobilization and point system is based on two cardinal principles, the first of which is that military requirements must override all other considerations and, second, that the arrangements for the release of men from the forces must be such as will be readily understood and accepted as fair by the forces, and not be too complicated for practical application. All soldiers were given handbooks clear and definite.
Our soldiers have been handed booklets. During the summer months I received one of those booklets, and I found it most interesting. One booklet was issued by the Department of Veterans Affairs, and I found it most instructive. It contained a great deal of valuable information. But, so far as getting shipping to bring the boys back to Canada is concerned, it was the most-complicated information I have ever seen.
I might say that more than two-thirds of my time daily in the last six years have been spent in dealing with these matters. I find, however, that one can get very little relief, nor can he find out what is going on. No soldier can find the proper telephone to locate officers on demobilization. The federal telephones in our Toronto book are all mixed up and I have had this trouble myself and sometimes try many wrong numbers in vain. I have complained to the Minister of Public 47696-108J
Works and to the ministers in other departments, but one finds great difficulty in reaching them by telephone, or the right office. For instance, last Saturday I tried to look into a matter of this kind. First I rang one telephone and- then another and then another, and then another and, after an hour and a half I gave up and had to write to the department here about it.
I hold in my hand one of the booklets which was handed out last night. I know something about the information contained therein. I know something of the wonderful war record and work of Lieutenant General Simmonds, Major General Vokes, and Lieutenant General Crerar. I know something of their families for many years past and their patriotism since school days. Up until early summer I had confidence that this point system might have operated. However, it has not. The system now offered has not been brought up to date,' and no better system has been proposed.
The British system is less complicated, because they make their selections according to age and length of service, and make selections for those who will be engaged in reconstruction work. Then, there have been many changes in their scheme.
Away back on August 22 Mr. Churchill, as leader of the opposition, made a speech in the House of Commons in England on this matter in which he urged that changes be made, and it be speeded up to aid reconversion and reconstruction. The announcement was made that British shipping would be made available for British soldiers to return them-and I assume that that is why our Prime Minister said in London that he was trying to get more shipping and devise quicker demobilization.
Back in July I complained about ships being given back to France, and United States soldiers securing sixty per cent of British transport. I pointed out that the Prime Minister was making negotiations for shipping. However, thus far we have not heard anything so far in this debate about what our Prime Minister has done. He has been in England for some time and nobody seems to know what is being done in this matter, except from cables in the press.
We are having the utmost difficulty also when the men return. Away back last September I asked this question on the order paper:
What has been done to help ex-servicemen who wish to reopen their retail shops?
I asked the question, because there were no shops to be had. A return was ordered. The reply I received from the wartime prices and trade board on October 18 was a lengthy
Demobilization-Army

one, and one which nobody could understand. That is the way our boys are being used when they get home-no shops available and irksome controls to block them.
The system is all wrong. The war was brought to a sudden conclusion and the government was not ready after Germany's collapse. The defeat of Japan brought the war to a close much more quickly. But it was not concluded through any miracle, but only through the powerful effort of all the allies. It is ridiculous to believe that the atomic bomb can eliminate ground fighting. The sensational advent of the bomb has blinded some people to the point where they believe that it is a complete answer. Once again in this, as in every war, people have been shocked and stupified by surprise. I say that no one weapon can revolutionize war. No such weapon has been found up to this time. It will always be the superior force which will beat down the enemy.
There may be opportunity at another time to say something. In closing, I would say this to the government, that most of our ships in the battle of the Atlantic would have gone to the bottom of the sea, had it not been for one important element, the great bridgehead to America by water. I should like to see the Prime Minister do the same as their majesties did, as Mr. Churchill did, and as President Roosevelt and his successor did. He should go to the bridgehead we had at Ulster and pay a tribute to those people who during this war dad so much to save our citizens and our sailors and get supplies to the battle lines.

Since the estimates are being disposed of so rapidly I just wanted to remind the minister that he promised to answer a number of questions at the time the naval estimates were being considered. These are to be found on pages 1526 and 1565~of Hansard. I see quite a few answers going through and I hope he has not slipped up on these.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I thought it would be better to dean up all my naval information at one time in order that it could be properly indexed in Hansard. I have not all the information as yet.

Many of these men who were sentenced for desertion or other misdemeanours are mechanics of one kind or another? I know myself that a number of these men are plumbers, steamfitters and so on, tradesmen that are in great demand at the moment. Could not a system of ticket-of-leave be set up so that these men could be released?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall be glad to look into that. I have had numerous representations on the same score, particularly with respect to badly needed farm workers and other workers who it was claimed were essential in the construction industry. So far it has been felt that it was not feasible in the interests of discipline to release ahead of his .turn a particular man who happened to be skilled in a particular trade. Perhaps the time has now come to reconsider the policy, and I shall be glad to take his suggestion into consideration and discuss it with, the members of my staff.

I have in mind the son
of a master plumber who is overwhelmed with work. This son is an expert plumber but he was one of those unfortunate boys who served in the front line but who apparently lost their nerve. He was sentenced for desertion. I shall hot take up the time of the committee now in discussing this case but I will let the [DOT]minister have the particulars. My thought right along has been that if at all possible such men might be released under a programme similar to the civilian ticket-of-leave.

A while ago I
raised the question of the segregation of these prisoners and removing them from the penitentiaries and penal institutions. What is the minister's view with regard to that? That is a matter upon which we should have some assurance this afternoon. There is also the question of the legality of imprisoning these men in penal institutions. I think the point raised by the hon. member for Cape Breton South has considerable merit.
I know that in connection with army matters the procedure is somewhat loose on occasion. Only recently I had a discussion with a provost marshal who pointed out that prisoners were being sent from one province to another without the proper authority of the officer commanding at the point from which the prisoners were being sent. This is a matter upon which we should have an opinion from the law officers of the crown. Whether or-not these men are legally incarcerated, the fact remains that a great stigma will attach to them throughout the remainder of their lives because of having been imprisoned in penitentiaries for offences that were non-criminal within the meaning of the criminal code. The minister should be in position to give an answer in regard to that matter.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
First, as to the question of the legality of sending men who have been condemned by military courts to a term of imprisonment to civilian institutions. I would not care to give my personal opinion on that. I think it would be proper that I should

Demobilization-Army
obtain, the opinion either of the Department of Justice or of the legal officers of my own department.
As to whether it is proper to confine men who have committed purely military offences, such as desertion and the like, in civilian penitentiaries, again I would prefer not to express a personal opinion until I have had an opportunity of discussing the matter with the officers of my department and getting a little more clearly in my own mind why it is being done. I will give my hon. friend that answer to-morrow.

I have just one more question as to the general set-up. These men are being placed in penitentiaries and penal institutions under orders of courts martial. The minister has gone part of the way. He has set up a board with powers similar to that of the remission branch, but I do not think that goes far enough. The complaints which I receive are that these men did not have a proper opportunity to place their defences before the courts martial. I have a case in mind of a military officer who was dismissed from the service for an offence alleged to have been committed in Belgium. He was entitled under the law to a precis of the offence and the circumstances surrounding its commission and also of the defence, if any, to the military crime with which he was charged. He was given a counsel but he did not have more than five minutes to go over the facts with him. He claims that he received an unfair and unjust trial in that he had no one to represent him who was fully conversant with the facts or, as a matter of fact, conversant at all.
That is the general complaint. I mentioned a case a while ago of a young man who received a sentence of three years. He claims that when he appeared before the court martial a counsel was allotted to him but he had no opportunity of going over the facts with him. There is a suggestion of a grave miscarriage of justice. It might not be possible to provide for an appeal in all these cases; but where circumstances are brought to the attention of the minister or of the governor in council to indicate that there has been a serious miscarriage, should not an investigation of the case be proceeded with? Under the present set-up under Mr. Justice Mackay, all that will happen will be an examination of the record with a view to ascertaining whether there are extenuating circumstances. There will be no opportunity for a man who claims that his trial was unfair to have his case reviewed. While perhaps there should not be an appeal in all cases, some provision should be made so that when
circumstances are brought to the attention of the minister indicating the possibility or the probability of an injustice, a committee or a commission would be set up, with representatives of the accused or the appellant, so that all the facts may be properly brought before the board and no case of injustice permitted to remain on the record.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend that every effort should be made to see that no case of injustice remains on the record, as he puts it. He is a lawyer of long experience, and he knows it is not infrequent that an accused who has been condemned feels that his trial was perhaps not entirely fair, that he was not as well defended as he should have been or that all the evidence which should have been placed before the court was not placed before the court. In civil procedure there are well defined rules of appeal whereby a case can be reopened. As my hon. friend knows, there is a somewhat similar procedure in military law. There is an appeal to the minister. If the minister confirms the decision of the court martial, there is an appeal to the governor in council. Cases of this kind have come before me in my short experience as minister, and I have sent them back for further investigation of the facts. Perhaps, as my hon. friend suggests, we should go a bit farther and have some outside board to which I could refer such cases in my discretion for a hearing. But frankly I would be reluctant to set up completely new appeal procedure and provide for an appeal of right from every finding of a court martial. That was not, I know, what my hon. friend suggested, but he will appreciate that it is hard to draw the line. What he suggested was that the board should be one to which cases might be referred in the discretion of somebody.
In the discretion of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It imposes certain responsibility on the minister. I might welcome- I am thinking aloud now-'being able to exercise that discretion. All I will say is that I will give the suggestion most careful consideration and discuss it with the officers of the department, who have had a good deal of experience in matters of this kind, and see whether some procedure of that sort may be adopted1. The function to be performed would, of course, be completely different from the one performed by the board of review. It would, in effect, be a new appeal tribunal.

Mr. Chairman, something has been said this afternoon about deserters. In this connection I wish to direct
Demobilization-Army

a few questions to the minister. Could he tell me whether the wives and children of soldiers under detention are in receipt of their allowances?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No. They are paid their allowance for six months after the detention has started, after which they do not receive anything.

I thank the minister for his answer.
Can he tell me what is the amount of such unpaid allowances for 1944-45 or 1943-44, that is to say for the last year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall have to obtain those figures from the officers who deal with expenditures and I shall be in a position to give them to the hon. member to-morrow.
Can the minister tell me what use is made of such funds when soldiers' allowances are not paid.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not understand the question.
I am informed that the moneys coming to the soldier while he is in detention go to the canteen fund.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No, that is not correct.

I have taken so little part in these discussions that I think I may be pardoned for saying a word in support of what has been said by the hon. member for Lake Centre. I have brought on.e or two cases to the attention of the minister, and I have had word from him that he is having an investigation made. I do not know whether this is what the hon. member for Lake Centre had in mind, but what I am afraid of is that too legalistic an approach is being made in these cases. There are emotional factors too, which generals and lawyers are not likely to take into consideration, and I think that is what is needed in these cases.
A case came to my attention of a man who deserted after he had been for a long time in the front line, was wounded and sent back again when it was considered by some of his officers he was not fit for duty. He deserted for a very short period. He was later convicted, so far as I know, on the evidence of the medical officer who did not even look at him but prescribed some pills or something of that kind. The man is now serving two years in military barracks at Vancouver. There are many cases of that kind, and I think that the minister should try to get something which is just a little more than the formal cold decision of a mil'tary court and legal proce-

dure. Otherwise I am afraid that grave injustice may be done. If anything that I may say would help to convince the minister that something along these lines should be done, I say it now, and I hope that he will give it more than mere consideration.
Progress reported.
